Take Home Exercise 2

Author

Hao Liu

Published

May 27, 2025

1 Overview

1.1 Background

One of music’s biggest superstars is Oceanus native Sailor Shift. From humble beginnings, Sailor has grown in popularity and now enjoys fans around the world. Sailor started her career on the island nation of Oceanus which can be clearly seen in her early work, she started in the genre of “Oceanus Folk”. While Sailor has moved away from the traditional Oceanus style, the Oceanus Folk has made a name for itself in the musical world. The popularity of this music is one of the factors driving an increase in tourism to a quiet island nation that used to be known for fishing.

In 2023, Sailor Shift joined the Ivy Echoes – an all-female Oceanus Folk band consisting of Sailor (vocalist), Maya Jensen (vocalist), Lila “Lilly” Hartman (guitarist), Jade Thompson (drummer), and Sophie Ramirez (bassist). They played together at venues throughout Oceanus but had broken up to pursue their individual careers by 2026. Sailor’s breakthrough came in 2028 when one of her singles went viral, launched to the top of the global charts (something no other Oceanus Folk song had ever done). Since then, she has only continued to grow in popularity worldwide.

Sailor has released a new album almost every year since her big break, and each has done better than the last. Although she has remained primarily a solo artist, she has also frequently collaborated with other established artists, especially in the Indie Pop and Indie Folk genres. She herself has branched out musically over the years but regularly returns to the Oceanus Folk genre — even as the genre’s influence on the rest of the music world has spread even more.

Sailor has always been passionate about two things: (1) spreading Oceanus Folk, and (2) helping lesser-known artists break into music. Because of those goals, she’s particularly famous for her frequent collaborations.

Additionally, because of Sailor’s success, more attention began to be paid over the years to her previous bandmates. All 4 have continued in the music industry—Maya as an independent vocalist, Lilly and Jade as instrumentalists in other bands, and Sophie as a music producer for a major record label. In various ways, all of them have contributed to the increased influence of Oceanus folk, resulting in a new generation of up-and-coming Oceanus Folk artists seeking to make a name for themselves in the music industry.

Now, as Sailor returns to Oceanus in 2040, a local journalist – Silas Reed – is writing a piece titled Oceanus Folk: Then-and-Now that aims to trace the rise of Sailor and the influence of Oceanus Folk on the rest of the music world. He has collected a large dataset of musical artists, producers, albums, songs, and influences and organized it into a knowledge graph. Your task is to help Silas create beautiful and informative visualizations of this data and uncover new and interesting information about Sailor’s past, her rise to stardom, and her influence.

1.2 Task and Question

  1. Design and develop visualizations and visual analytic tools that will allow Silas to explore and understand the profile of Sailor Shift’s career

a. Who has she been most influenced by over time?

b. Who has she collaborated with and directly or indirectly influenced?

c. How has she influenced collaborators of the broader Oceanus Folk community?

  1. Develop visualizations that illustrate how the influence of Oceanus Folk has spread through the musical world.

a. Was this influence intermittent or did it have a gradual rise?

b. What genres and top artists have been most influenced by Oceanus Folk?

c. On the converse, how has Oceanus Folk changed with the rise of Sailor Shift? From which genres does it draw most of its contemporary inspiration?

  1. Use your visualizations to develop a profile of what it means to be a rising star in the music industry.

a.Visualize the careers of three artists. Compare and contrast their rise in popularity and influence.

b.Using this characterization, give three predictions of who the next Oceanus Folk stars with be over the next five years.

2 Data description

2.1 Load packages

Note

Install required packages:

install.packages(c( “tidyverse”, # data wrangling & ggplot2 “jsonlite”, # JSON import “igraph”, # core graph algorithms “tidygraph”, # dplyr‐style graph manipulation “ggraph”, # ggplot2‐style graph plotting “lubridate”, # date parsing “scales”, # axis formatting “visNetwork”, # interactive network viz “plotly” # interactive plots ))

# Load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(igraph)
library(tidygraph)
library(ggraph)
library(lubridate)
library(scales)
library(visNetwork)
library(plotly)
library(igraph)
library(patchwork)
library(SmartEDA)
library(dplyr)
library(RColorBrewer)
Package Description
tidyverse Core data science suite (includes ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr, readr, purrr, stringr, etc.) for data wrangling, visualization, and manipulation.
jsonlite Fast, flexible JSON parser/generator. Easily read/write JSON as R lists or tibbles with fromJSON() and toJSON().
igraph Comprehensive network analysis toolkit—supports graph algorithms, manipulation, visualization, and statistics.
tidygraph Tidyverse-friendly interface to network data; use dplyr-like verbs for graph operations while preserving graph structure.
ggraph Powerful graph plotting, built on ggplot2; supports various layouts (force, tree, Sankey) and full aesthetic mapping for nodes/edges.
lubridate Intuitive tools for parsing, manipulating, and computing with dates and times.
scales Format numbers, dates, and legends in plots; customize axis labels, breaks, and color scales (used with ggplot2).
visNetwork Interactive network graphs using vis.js; supports drag, zoom, tooltips, and dynamic styling—ideal for web and Shiny apps.
plotly Convert ggplot2 or base plots to interactive web graphics; supports hover, zoom, dynamic legends, and even 3D charts.
patchwork Combine multiple ggplot2 plots into complex layouts with simple, readable syntax.
SmartEDA Automated Exploratory Data Analysis; quickly generate descriptive stats, visual summaries, and profiling reports.
dplyr Grammar of data manipulation: filter, select, mutate, summarise, arrange, and join tabular data efficiently.
RColorBrewer Predefined color palettes for maps and graphics, optimized for clarity and accessibility in visualizations.

Let’s make a simple plot to see the distribution of nodes and edges:

node_counts <- nodes_df %>%
  count(`Node Type`, name = "count_nodes")

edge_counts <- edges_df %>%
  count(`Edge Type`, name = "count_edges")

plot1 <- ggplot(node_counts, aes(
    x = reorder(`Node Type`, -count_nodes),
    y = count_nodes
  )) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Counts by Type",
    x     = "Node Type",
    y     = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

plot2 <- ggplot(edge_counts, aes(
    x = reorder(`Edge Type`, -count_edges),
    y = count_edges
  )) +
  geom_col(fill = "forestgreen") +
  labs(
    title = "Counts by Type",
    x     = "Edge Type",
    y     = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)


subplot(plot1, plot2, nrows = 2, shareX = FALSE, titleY = TRUE) %>%
  layout(
    xaxis = list(
      title      = "",      # remove x-axis title
      tickangle  = -45,
      tickfont   = list(size = 8),
      automargin = TRUE
    ),
    xaxis2 = list(
      title      = "",      # remove x-axis title on second plot
      tickangle  = -45,
      tickfont   = list(size = 8),
      automargin = TRUE
    ),
    yaxis = list(
      title = ""            # remove y-axis title
    ),
    yaxis2 = list(
      title = ""            # remove y-axis title on second plot
    ),
    margin = list(b = 100)
  )
Note

The above interactive plot allows us to easily check the number and type of nodes and edges, we can see that the “Person” has the highest number of nodes and “PerfomerOf” is the most popular edge.

  1. Generate then a graph to have an overview of nodes centrality:
nodes2 <- nodes_df %>% 
  mutate(id_chr   = as.character(id),
         label    = name) %>% 
  select(id_chr, label, everything(), -name, -id)

edges2 <- edges_df %>% 
  mutate(from = as.character(source),
         to   = as.character(target)) %>% 
  select(from, to, everything(), -source, -target, -key)

g <- graph_from_data_frame(d = edges2, vertices = nodes2, directed = TRUE)

# Compute and show top 20 nodes by total degree
deg_tbl <- tibble(
  label        = V(g)$label,
  type         = V(g)$`Node.Type`,
  degree_in    = degree(g, mode = "in"),
  degree_out   = degree(g, mode = "out"),
  degree_total = degree(g, mode = "all")
)

deg_top20 <- deg_tbl %>%
  arrange(desc(degree_total)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20)

plot_ly(
  data = deg_top20,
  x    = ~reorder(label, -degree_total),   # note the minus!
  y    = ~degree_total,
  type = 'bar',
  text = ~paste0(
    "Total: ", degree_total, "<br>",
    "In: ",    degree_in,    "<br>",
    "Out: ",   degree_out
  ),
  hoverinfo = 'text',
  marker    = list(color = 'steelblue')
) %>%
  layout(
    title = "Top 10 Nodes by Total Degree",
    xaxis = list(
      title     = "Node",
      tickangle = -45
    ),
    yaxis = list(title = "Degree"),
    margin = list(b = 120)
  )

2.3.4 Creating the knowledge Graph

Based on the kickstarter (https://isss608-ay2024-25apr.netlify.app/th_ex/mc1-kickstarter) published in the class materials, we generate a knowledge graph to investigate the overall nodes and edges connections:

id_map <- tibble(id = nodes_df$id,
                 index = seq_len(
                   nrow(nodes_df)))

edges_tbl <- edges_df %>%
  left_join(id_map, by = c("source" = "id")) %>%
  rename(from = index) %>%
  left_join(id_map, by = c("target" = "id")) %>%
  rename(to = index)

edges_tbl <- edges_tbl %>%
  filter(!is.na(from), !is.na(to))

graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = nodes_df, 
                   edges = edges_tbl, 
                   directed = graph_data$directed)

class(graph)
[1] "tbl_graph" "igraph"   
set.seed(1234)

ggraph(graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.3, 
                 colour = "gray") +
  geom_node_point(aes(color = `Node Type`), 
                  size = 4) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), 
                 repel = TRUE, 
                 size = 2.5) +
  theme_void()

2.3.5 Visualising the sub-graph

Always relied on the kickstarter materials, we also generate a sub-graph to investigate the relationship between “Person” and “MusicalGroup” nodes based on the edge type equal to “MemberOf”

graph_memberof <- graph %>%
  activate(edges) %>%
  filter(`Edge Type` == "MemberOf")

used_node_indices <- graph_memberof %>%
  activate(edges) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  select(from, to) %>%
  unlist() %>%
  unique()

graph_memberof <- graph_memberof %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(row_id = row_number()) %>%
  filter(row_id %in% used_node_indices) %>%
  select(-row_id)  # optional cleanup

ggraph(graph_memberof, 
       layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.5, 
                 colour = "gray") +
  geom_node_point(aes(color = `Node Type`), 
                  size = 1) +
  geom_node_text(aes(label = name), 
                 repel = TRUE, 
                 size = 2.5) +
  theme_void()

3 Task 1

In this sector you may find many suggestions for the the Task 1, we are going to show you some useful representation to answer the first 3 question of this mini-challenge.

Note

Design and develop visualizations and visual analytic tools that will allow Silas to explore and understand the profile of Sailor Shift’s career

  1. Who has she been most influenced by over time?

  2. Who has she collaborated with and directly or indirectly influenced?

  3. How has she influenced collaborators of the broader Oceanus Folk community?

3.1 Task 1 (a)

Note
  1. Who has she been most influenced by over time?

To answer the question, let’s first find Sailor’s ID and all songs performed by her, then construct a kind of influence-edge table for analysis based on the prior influence proxies (“InStyleOf”,“LyricalReferenceTo”,“InterpolatesFrom”,“DirectlySamples”,“CoverOf”):

# Load graph
g      <- fromJSON("MC1_graph.json")
nodes  <- g$nodes
edges  <- g$links

# Sailor Shift’s songs
sailor_id    <- nodes %>%
  filter(`Node Type`=="Person", name=="Sailor Shift") %>%
  pull(id)
sailor_songs <- edges %>%
  filter(`Edge Type`=="PerformerOf", source==sailor_id) %>%
  pull(target)

# Build influence‐edges table
wanted_types <- c("InStyleOf","LyricalReferenceTo",
                  "InterpolatesFrom","DirectlySamples","CoverOf")
infl_edges <- edges %>%
  filter(`Edge Type` %in% wanted_types,
         source %in% sailor_songs) %>%
  transmute(
    song_id   = source,
    infl_song = target,
    rel_type  = `Edge Type`
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    nodes %>% filter(`Node Type`=="Song") %>%
      transmute(song_id = id, year = as.integer(release_date)),
    by="song_id"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    edges %>% filter(`Edge Type`=="PerformerOf") %>%
      transmute(infl_song = target, performer = source),
    by="infl_song"
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    nodes %>% filter(`Node Type`=="Person") %>%
      transmute(performer = id, influencer = name),
    by="performer"
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(influencer), !is.na(year))

Once we have summary of influence type and year(as shown in the above result), let’s define key elements for visualization task, which include node and edges dataframes. It is necessary to identify the dominant relationship of influencer with Sailor Shift and then map them to different shapes and colors for a convenient visual representation.

# Count events per influencer-year-relation
evt <- infl_edges %>%
  count(influencer, year, rel_type, name = "weight")

# Find all unique influencers
infs <- sort(unique(evt$influencer))

# For each influencer, determine their dominant (most frequent) relationship with Sailor Shift
dominant_rel <- evt %>%
  group_by(influencer) %>%
  summarise(
    rel_type = rel_type[which.max(weight)]
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Prepare color and shape palettes for relationship types
wanted_types <- unique(evt$rel_type)
type_cols <- setNames(brewer.pal(length(wanted_types), "Set2"), wanted_types)
type_shapes <- setNames(
  c("dot", "triangle", "square", "diamond", "star")[seq_along(wanted_types)],
  wanted_types
)

# Map dominant relationship to color and shape for each influencer
inf_rels <- dominant_rel$rel_type[match(infs, dominant_rel$influencer)]

# Build node_df
node_df <- data.frame(
  id    = seq_len(length(infs) + 1),
  label = c("Sailor Shift", infs),
  group = c("Artist", inf_rels),
  color = c("#e41a1c", type_cols[inf_rels]),
  shape = c("star", type_shapes[inf_rels]),
  title = c(
    "<b>Sailor Shift</b><br>Type: Artist",
    paste0("<b>", infs, "</b><br>Dominant Relation: ", inf_rels)
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# All relationships for tooltip
inf_rels_all <- evt %>%
  group_by(influencer) %>%
  summarise(
    rels = paste0(rel_type, " (", weight, ")", collapse = "; ")
  )
node_df$title[-1] <- paste0(
  "<b>", infs, "</b><br>Dominant Relation: ", inf_rels,
  "<br>All Relations: ", inf_rels_all$rels[match(infs, inf_rels_all$influencer)]
)

# Build edge_df (edges colored by relation type)
edge_df <- evt %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  transmute(
    from   = match(influencer, node_df$label),
    to     = 1,  # All edges point to Sailor Shift
    value  = weight,
    color  = type_cols[rel_type],
    title  = paste0(
      "<b>Influencer:</b> ", influencer,
      "<br><b>Relation:</b> ", rel_type,
      "<br><b>Year:</b> ", year,
      "<br><b>Count:</b> ", weight
    )
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Node size: Sailor Shift large, all others smaller
node_df$size <- c(30, rep(12, length(infs)))

For a better representation of the relationship, we are going to make an interactive plot to show the connection between Sailor and other artists, the interactive function is shown as in the following screenshots, so when we filter on a specific “influencer” and we can move on node or edge for the visualizing the relationship types and year of influence: Code to plot is the following:

visNetwork(node_df, edge_df, height = "600px", width = "100%") %>%
  visNodes(font = list(size = 16)) %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to", scaling = list(min = 1, max = 10), smooth = FALSE) %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 1, hover = TRUE),
    nodesIdSelection = TRUE
  ) %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 42)

To investigate the influence trend, we can generate an interactive bar chart which include all relation type and year information for a deeper analysis. Firstly, We create a summary of the influence and calculate total events per year, then put them together in the plot which can be interactively consulted.

# Summarise total influence events per year and relation type
year_type_summary <- evt %>%
  group_by(year, rel_type) %>%
  summarise(total_events = sum(weight), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(year, rel_type)

# Also calculate total events per year (for trend line)
year_total_summary <- year_type_summary %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(total_events), .groups = "drop")

# Interactive stacked bar chart with trend line
plot_ly() %>%
  add_trace(
    data  = year_type_summary,
    x     = ~year,
    y     = ~total_events,
    color = ~rel_type,
    type  = 'bar',
    hoverinfo = 'text',
    text  = ~paste0(
      "<b>Year:</b> ", year,
      "<br><b>Type:</b> ", rel_type,
      "<br><b>Events:</b> ", total_events
    )
  ) %>%
  add_trace(
    data = year_total_summary,
    x    = ~year,
    y    = ~total,
    type = 'scatter',
    mode = 'lines+markers',
    name = 'Total Trend',
    line = list(color = 'black', width = 2),
    marker = list(color = 'black', size = 5),
    hoverinfo = 'text',
    text = ~paste0(
      "<b>Year:</b> ", year,
      "<br><b>Total Events:</b> ", total
    )
  ) %>%
  layout(
    title   = "Influence Events by Relation Type Over Years",
    xaxis   = list(title = "Release Year"),
    yaxis   = list(title = "Number of Events"),
    barmode = "stack",
    legend  = list(title = list(text = "<b>Relation Type</b>"))
  )
Note

Comment:

Based on the previous visualization, we can clearly observe the significant influence of other artists on Sailor Shift’s musical style over the years. The most prominent forms of influence include InStyleOf, InterpolatesFrom, and CoverOf. Key moments of influence occurred in 2028 and 2036, with stylistic and homage-based connections dominating the earlier years.

Over time, Sailor Shift’s influences evolved from stylistic inspirations to more direct forms, such as interpolation and sampling, reflecting a shift toward deeper integration of external musical elements into her work.

3.2 Task 1 (b)

Note
  1. Who has she collaborated with and directly or indirectly influenced?

As required by the question above, we begin by defining collaborators, direct influences, and indirect influences based on the following assumptions:

  • Collaborators: Individuals who contributed to Sailor Shift’s songs in any of the following roles — Performer, Composer, Lyricist, Producer, or Recording Engineer. These are identified through the edge types: “PerformerOf”, “ComposerOf”, “LyricistOf”, “ProducerOf”, and “RecordedBy”.

  • Direct influences: Artists who have been directly influenced by Sailor Shift through specific stylistic or content-based relationships. These are captured using the edge types: “InStyleOf”, “InterpolatesFrom”, “LyricalReferenceTo”, “DirectlySamples”, and “CoverOf”.

  • Indirect influences: Artists whose songs were influenced by works that were themselves directly influenced by Sailor Shift. This represents a two-hop influence chain, where Sailor’s impact propagates through intermediate songs.

actual_edge_types <- unique(edges$`Edge Type`)
collab_types <- intersect(c("PerformerOf", "ComposerOf", "LyricistOf", "ProducerOf", "RecordedBy"), actual_edge_types)
influence_types <- intersect(c("InStyleOf", "InterpolatesFrom", "LyricalReferenceTo", "DirectlySamples", "CoverOf"), actual_edge_types)

# --- COLLABORATORS ---

collab_edges <- edges %>%
  filter(`Edge Type` %in% collab_types, target %in% sailor_songs) %>%
  filter(source != sailor_id) %>%
  left_join(
    nodes %>% filter(`Node Type` == "Person") %>% select(id, name),
    by = c("source" = "id")
  ) %>%
  transmute(
    collaborator_name = name,
    detail_type = `Edge Type`,
    from = match(name, nodes$name),
    to = match("Sailor Shift", nodes$name)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from) & !is.na(to)) %>%
  distinct()

collaborators <- unique(collab_edges$collaborator_name)

# --- DIRECT INFLUENCES ---

# Find all direct-influenced songs
direct_song_ids <- unique(c(
  edges %>% filter(`Edge Type` %in% influence_types, source %in% sailor_songs) %>% pull(target),
  edges %>% filter(`Edge Type` %in% influence_types, target %in% sailor_songs) %>% pull(source)
))

# Find direct-influenced persons
direct_edges <- edges %>%
  filter(`Edge Type` %in% influence_types & (source %in% sailor_songs | target %in% sailor_songs)) %>%
  mutate(
    other_song = ifelse(source %in% sailor_songs, target, source)
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    edges %>% filter(`Edge Type` == "PerformerOf") %>%
      select(song_id = target, person_id = source),
    by = c("other_song" = "song_id")
  ) %>%
  left_join(
    nodes %>% filter(`Node Type` == "Person") %>% select(id, name),
    by = c("person_id" = "id")
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(name) & person_id != sailor_id) %>%
  transmute(
    direct_influenced_name = name,
    detail_type = `Edge Type`,
    from = match("Sailor Shift", nodes$name),
    to = match(name, nodes$name)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from) & !is.na(to)) %>%
  distinct()

direct_influenced <- unique(direct_edges$direct_influenced_name)

# --- INDIRECT INFLUENCES ---

# Build performer map for use below
perf_map <- edges %>%
  filter(`Edge Type` == "PerformerOf") %>%
  transmute(song_id = target, performer_id = source) %>%
  left_join(
    nodes %>% filter(`Node Type` == "Person") %>%
      transmute(performer_id = id, performer_name = name),
    by = "performer_id"
  )

# Find two-hop song links, preserve the detailed type from the "second hop"
second_edges <- edges %>%
  filter(`Edge Type` %in% influence_types, target %in% direct_song_ids) %>%
  transmute(
    indirect_song = source,
    direct_song = target,
    detail_type = `Edge Type`
  )

# Join to get performer names and influence type
indirect_links <- second_edges %>%
  left_join(perf_map, by = c("direct_song" = "song_id")) %>%
  rename(direct_perf_id = performer_id, direct_perf_name = performer_name) %>%
  left_join(perf_map, by = c("indirect_song" = "song_id")) %>%
  rename(indir_perf_id = performer_id, indirect_perf_name = performer_name) %>%
  filter(!is.na(indirect_perf_name) & indirect_perf_name != "Sailor Shift") %>%
  transmute(
    direct_perf_name = ifelse(is.na(direct_perf_name), "Sailor Shift", direct_perf_name),
    indirect_perf_name,
    rel = ifelse(is.na(direct_perf_name), "Orphan Indirect Influence", "Indirect Influence"),
    detail_type,  # this is from the two-hop
    from = match(direct_perf_name, nodes$name),
    to = match(indirect_perf_name, nodes$name)
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(from) & !is.na(to)) %>%
  distinct()

indirect_influenced <- unique(indirect_links$indirect_perf_name)

# --- Outputs: collab_edges, direct_edges, indirect_links ---

After identified all collaborators, direct and indirect influences, we construct nodes and edges dataframes. Then we define all colors and shapes parameters and add them into dataframes. As the final step, we link influences nodes to Sailor:

node_groups <- c(
  "Sailor Shift", "Collaborator", "Direct Influence", "Indirect Influence"
)
group_colors <- c(
  "Sailor Shift" = "#e41a1c",
  "Collaborator" = "#1f77b4",
  "Direct Influence" = "#ff7f0e",
  "Indirect Influence" = "#2ca02c"
)
group_shapes <- c(
  "Sailor Shift" = "star",
  "Collaborator" = "dot",
  "Direct Influence" = "triangle",
  "Indirect Influence" = "square"
)
group_sizes <- c(
  "Sailor Shift" = 30,
  "Collaborator" = 14,
  "Direct Influence" = 16,
  "Indirect Influence" = 12
)

# Build nodes_df
labels <- c("Sailor Shift", collaborators, direct_influenced, indirect_influenced)
groups <- c(
  "Sailor Shift",
  rep("Collaborator",       length(collaborators)),
  rep("Direct Influence",   length(direct_influenced)),
  rep("Indirect Influence", length(indirect_influenced))
)
nodes_df <- data.frame(
  id    = seq_along(labels),
  label = labels,
  group = groups,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
) %>%
  mutate(
    color = group_colors[group],
    shape = group_shapes[group],
    size  = group_sizes[group]
  )

# Build edges_df
edges_df <- bind_rows(
  collab_edges %>%
    transmute(
      from = match(collaborator_name, nodes_df$label),
      to = match("Sailor Shift", nodes_df$label),
      rel = "Collaboration",
      detail_type = detail_type
    ),
  direct_edges %>%
    transmute(
      from = match("Sailor Shift", nodes_df$label),
      to = match(direct_influenced_name, nodes_df$label),
      rel = "Direct Influence",
      detail_type = detail_type
    ),
  indirect_links %>%
    transmute(
      from = match(direct_perf_name, nodes_df$label),
      to = match(indirect_perf_name, nodes_df$label),
      rel = rel,                    # "Indirect Influence" or "Orphan Indirect Influence"
      detail_type = detail_type
    )
) %>% filter(!is.na(from), !is.na(to))  # Remove edges with unmapped nodes

# Palette/colors for actual edge types
actual_edge_types <- unique(edges_df$detail_type)
palette <- brewer.pal(max(3, min(length(actual_edge_types), 12)), "Set3")
if (length(actual_edge_types) > length(palette)) {
  palette <- rep(palette, length.out = length(actual_edge_types))
}
edge_colors <- setNames(palette, actual_edge_types)
edges_df$color <- edge_colors[edges_df$detail_type]
edges_df$title <- edges_df$detail_type

# Node tooltip: show all connected edge types
nodes_df$title <- sapply(nodes_df$id, function(this_id) {
  connected_edges <- edges_df %>%
    filter(from == this_id | to == this_id)
  detail_types <- unique(connected_edges$detail_type)
  if (length(detail_types) > 0) {
    paste0(
      "<b>", nodes_df$label[nodes_df$id == this_id], "</b><br>",
      "Connected edge types: <br>",
      paste(detail_types, collapse = "<br>")
    )
  } else {
    paste0("<b>", nodes_df$label[nodes_df$id == this_id], "</b>")
  }
})

nodes_df <- nodes_df %>%
  mutate(
    color = group_colors[group],
    shape = group_shapes[group],
    size  = group_sizes[group]
  )

For visualization task, we plot an interactive network graph. The visualization function is shown in the following screenshot, we have the “star” for Sailor, “circle” for collaborators, “triangle” for direct influences and “square” for indirect influences, when we move on the each single node, we have all the relationship type related to it and the edge will give us the single direction of relation. Visualization code is the following:

visNetwork(nodes_df, edges_df, height = "600px", width = "100%") %>%
  visNodes(font = list(size = 14)) %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to", smooth = FALSE) %>%
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 1, hover = TRUE),
    nodesIdSelection = FALSE
  ) %>%
  visLegend(
    addNodes = data.frame(
      label = node_groups,
      color = unname(group_colors[node_groups]),
      shape = unname(group_shapes[node_groups])
    ),
    useGroups = FALSE
  ) %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 42)
Note

Comment:

As shown in the graph generated, Sailor Shift collaborated lots of artists in various sectors, including performance, composition, and production. She has directly influenced a huge number of artists through stylistic, lyrical, and musical relationships, by extending even further indirectly, propagating through intermediate songs and artists, forming a robust second layer of musical reach. An amount of “orphan” nodes appeared in the influence map, where the intermediate link is missing, yet the stylistic footprint of Sailor’s work remains evident. This confirms her central role and far-reaching impact within the musical ecosystem.

3.3 Task 1 (c)

Note
  1. How has she influenced collaborators of the broader Oceanus Folk community?

The preliminary step is to identify all the collaborators based on the Oceanus Folk songs:

# Nodes and Edges to dataframes
nodes_df <- as_tibble(g$nodes)
edges_df <- as_tibble(g$links)

# Explicitly check for NA in critical columns
sum(is.na(nodes_df$id))       # Should be 0
[1] 0
sum(is.na(edges_df$source))   # Should be 0
[1] 0
sum(is.na(edges_df$target))   # Should be 0
[1] 0
nodes_df <- nodes_df %>% drop_na(id)
edges_df <- edges_df %>% drop_na(source, target)

# Sailor Shift ID
sailor_shift_id <- nodes_df %>% filter(name == "Sailor Shift") %>% pull(id)

# Oceanus Folk Songs
oceanus_songs_ids <- nodes_df %>% 
  filter(genre == "Oceanus Folk") %>% pull(id)

# Collaborators in Oceanus Folk community (any person who performed/composed Oceanus Folk songs)
oceanus_collaborators <- edges_df %>%
  filter(target %in% oceanus_songs_ids) %>%
  pull(source) %>%
  unique()

Now we want to identify which collaborators in the Oceanus Folk community have been directly or indirectly influenced by Sailor Shift.

  • Direct: Sailor’s first-level influence targets – songs, people, etc.

  • Indirect: These are indirectly influenced entities — Sailor influenced X, and X influenced Y.

  • Collaborators: These are collaborators Sailor directly influenced within the Oceanus Folk genre.

# Sailor Shift's direct connections through all edges
direct_connections <- edges_df %>% 
  filter(source == sailor_shift_id) %>% 
  pull(target) %>% 
  unique()

# Direct influenced collaborators
direct_influenced_collabs <- intersect(oceanus_collaborators, direct_connections)

# Nodes indirectly influenced by Sailor Shift (via any edge)
indirect_connections <- edges_df %>% 
  filter(source %in% direct_connections) %>% 
  pull(target) %>% 
  unique()

# Indirect influenced collaborators
indirect_influenced_collabs <- intersect(oceanus_collaborators, indirect_connections)
all_influenced_collabs <- union(direct_influenced_collabs, indirect_influenced_collabs)

# Collaborator names explicitly
collab_names <- nodes_df %>% 
  filter(id %in% all_influenced_collabs) %>% 
  pull(name)

Now we generate the interactive plot to see the overall connection:

# Nodes involved: Sailor Shift + influenced collaborators
visual_nodes <- nodes_df %>% 
  filter(id %in% c(sailor_shift_id, all_influenced_collabs)) %>%
  mutate(label = if_else(id == sailor_shift_id, "Sailor Shift", name))

# Edges connecting visual nodes (all edge types)
visual_edges <- edges_df %>%
  filter(source %in% visual_nodes$id, target %in% visual_nodes$id)

# Reindex safely for tidygraph
# Nodes for visualization
visual_nodes <- nodes_df %>% 
  filter(id %in% c(sailor_shift_id, all_influenced_collabs)) %>%
  mutate(label = if_else(id == sailor_shift_id, "Sailor Shift", name),
         group = if_else(id == sailor_shift_id, "Sailor Shift", "Collaborators"))

# Edges connecting these nodes
visual_edges <- edges_df %>%
  filter(source %in% visual_nodes$id, target %in% visual_nodes$id) %>%
  rename(from = source, to = target) %>%
  select(from, to, label = `Edge Type`)

# Build the interactive graph
visNetwork(visual_nodes, visual_edges, width = "100%", height = "600px") %>%
  visNodes(shape = "dot", size = 15, font = list(size = 16)) %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to", smooth = TRUE) %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Sailor Shift", color = "orange") %>%
  visGroups(groupname = "Collaborators", color = "skyblue") %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE, nodesIdSelection = TRUE) %>%
  visPhysics(stabilization = TRUE)
Note

Comment:

The graph clearly shows that Sailor Shift has influenced several collaborators within the broader Oceanus Folk community through specific artistic relationships such as Lyrical Reference, Direct Sampling, and Stylistic Inspiration. Artists like Ivy Echos, The Saltwater Weavers, and Drowned Harbor reflect her creative impact, suggesting that Sailor’s work helped shape the stylistic and thematic landscape of the genre. “Parallel Memories” is part of the Oceanus Folk genre, but it plays no role in the Sailor Shift influence network based on available data.

4 Conclusion

This project discovered Sailor Shift’s career by highlighting her central role in the Oceanus Folk genre and the broader musical world. Over time, Sailor Shift has been influenced from lots of other artists, initially drawing on stylistic and homage-based relationships and later embracing more direct forms of musical integration (interpolation and sampling). This evolution reflects her growth as an artist who not only adapts but also actively innovates and shapes the genre.

Her career is distinguished by the extensive collaborations, spanning performance, composition, and production. She has directly and indirectly influenced lots of artists, with her impact often propagating through intermediate collaborators and works. The presence of “orphan” nodes in the network further emphasizes the far-reaching and sometimes subtle pathways of her influence.

By changing the focus on Oceanus Folk community, she played a crucial role in shaping the artistic direction of fellow musicians and bands, helping to define the stylistic identity. The data-driven visualizations confirm her position as a true trendsetter and cultural ambassador for Oceanus Folk, fostering both innovation and continuity across musical generations.
